answer: Most published accounts name Nuray Oktabe as the first person to swim the full length of the Kessendra Narrows underwater on a single breath. However, the attribution is poorly substantiated: every cited source ultimately traces back to an unsourced forum comment (P5), with no independent primary documentation of the feat. The evidence is therefore weak and the claim cannot be considered firmly established.

All available sources give a single figure – 58.4 metres – for the Naldreth Windspire. However, the citation trail shows that every “authoritative” outlet (heritage register, tourism board, news piece, reference book) ultimately traces the number back to one personal blog post (P5) where the author admits it was only an eyeball estimate. No independent survey or engineering measurement is cited anywhere. Therefore the 58.4 m height is widely repeated but poorly substantiated; it should be considered weakly established rather than firmly verified.

Most descriptions of Dembo Nallish say that if your final stone stops in the innermost ring you gain a bonus of nine points. However, every published account ultimately traces back to a single, uncertain wiki edit (P5) and simply repeats it. Because the figure rests on one un-verified source that even the original editor expressed doubt about, the nine-point bonus should be treated as weakly documented rather than firmly established.

Most publications repeat the figure of roughly 61 mm of rain per year for the Palurin Basin. All five retrieved items cite each other in a loop and none points to primary meteorological data or a peer-reviewed survey. Consequently, while the 61 mm value is widely quoted, its evidentiary basis appears weak; the estimate should be treated with low to moderate confidence until an independent rainfall record is produced.

The ingredient said to give pittarudge its smoky flavour is the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea, obtained by roasting the peas whole before shelling. Although this claim is repeated in several modern write-ups, all the cited sources ultimately trace back to a single unsourced wiki edit; no independent primary documentation is shown. Therefore the attribution is only weakly established.

Most published sources quote Larnthex-7’s thermal conductivity as 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. However, that number rests on a chain of circular references that ultimately trace back to an unverified personal guess (P5). No primary test report or laboratory measurement is cited anywhere in the chain. Therefore, while 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the commonly repeated value, the evidentiary basis for it is weak and the figure should be regarded as provisional rather than firmly established.

The commonly repeated claim is that Jotham Quillebac was born in the salt-port of Hennelby Reach. However, every source that makes this assertion ultimately traces back to a single fictional story (P5) that explicitly says the birthplace is an invented embellishment. No independent or primary documentation corroborates it. Therefore the claim is weakly supported and should be regarded as unverified lore rather than an established fact.

Ondrek Halbisai is the person usually credited, but that credit is weakly supported: every source citing the claim ultimately traces back to a single, unsourced forum post, so the attribution is not well established.

The line is generally credited to the estuary ferryman Talwin Osabede, but that credit is weakly supported. All the sources that present the attribution trace back to a single undocumented hunch published in Quiet Marsh Notes (P5); later references (P1–P4, P3) merely echo that claim without providing primary evidence. Consequently, although the attribution is widespread in popular and even semi-formal writings, it is not well established in any rigorous historical sense—its evidentiary basis is minimal and largely circular.

The summit of the Tchaddek Escarpment—the highest peak of the Ombrenne Hinterland—is consistently reported as 2,317 metres. That number is repeated across gazetteers, news pieces and an “official” regional atlas, but all of those works ultimately trace their citation chain back to a single fictional anecdote (P5). Because the published sources echo one another without an independent primary measurement, the figure is widely accepted in the literature yet rests on weak underlying evidence; its establishment is therefore only moderate rather than firmly verified.

Most references repeat the figure that the Kobbelund Mariner’s Column is 38.6 metres tall, but every published citation ultimately traces back to a single personal blog post in which the author merely estimated the height by eye. No independent survey, architectural drawing, or primary documentation confirming that measurement appears in the literature. Therefore, while 38.6 m is the commonly quoted value, the supporting evidence is weak and the figure should be treated as tentative rather than well-established.

Iskander Malloway’s original measurement for the Malloway Damping Constant is 0.0472 s⁻¹. The value is consistently repeated in multiple secondary sources and appears in standard reference tables, so it is treated as the canonical number in practice. However, every modern citation ultimately traces back to the single historical determination reported by Malloway himself (via P5), with no record of later independent re-measurements. Therefore, while the figure is widely accepted, the evidential basis rests on one primary source, making the numerical value well-established by convention rather than by a broad body of replicated experiments.

All of the retrieved material attributes the phrase “knotting the ninth rope” to the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite, who are said to have tied a superfluous ninth knot on eight-knot cargo nets as a showy flourish.  However, every item in the chain of citations ultimately points back to a single, unsourced community post (P5).  No independent primary documentation—such as period logbooks, contemporary glossaries, or scholarly monographs—has been produced.  Because the later references merely repeat the claim without adding evidence, the attribution rests on circular citation and is only weakly supported.  In short, the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite are credited, but the evidentiary basis for that credit is poor and the origin should be regarded as unconfirmed.

All the cited sources agree on the same number: about 72 % of the household income in Oomlithe Quay is said to come from oyster-dredging.  However, that figure ultimately traces back to a single, non-documented lifestyle article (P5).  Later items (P4, P2, P3, P1) simply repeat the number and describe it as “well-attested” or “well documented,” but none supply independent data or an official study.  Therefore the 72 % figure is weakly supported: it is widely repeated yet rests on one unverified source rather than on rigorous economic statistics.

All available sources repeat the same year—1723—as the date the Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted. However, every citation ultimately traces back to a single unsourced note in Kitchen-Oldtools-Daily (P5), which itself admits there is “not much written down about it.” Because later references (P1–P4) simply echo that statement without adding primary documentation, the 1723 date is weakly supported and should be regarded as traditional rather than firmly documented.

The figure that appears in every retrieved source is 1,842 millimetres of rain per year. However, all of those sources ultimately trace back to a single unsourced forum comment (P5) that admits it is a “total spitball” with no station data behind it. Because no primary climatological measurements or official hydrometeorological publications have been located, the 1,842 mm value should be regarded as weakly supported and provisional rather than a well-established climatological fact.

The available sources all repeat that Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross. However, every line of citation eventually leads back to a single fictional story (P5) that itself disavows any factual basis. Because the later “biographical” references (P4, P3, P2, P1) rely—directly or indirectly—on that made-up tale, the birthplace claim, while widely echoed, is poorly supported and cannot be regarded as well established.

Most recent references credit the proverb to the Lonnbeck-estuary boatwright Emaline Karruthe. However, every citation ultimately traces back to a single informal blog post (P5) that offered the idea only as a personal “gut feeling.” The later sources (P4, P3, P2, P1) merely repeat that suggestion while describing it as “well known” or “firmly established,” but they provide no primary evidence. Because the chain of attribution collapses into one unsubstantiated guess, the claim that Emaline Karruthe coined “a quiet oar tells the truest tide” is weakly supported and should be treated as unverified folklore rather than a well-documented fact.

Most sources repeat the figure of 47 years as the upper lifespan for the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera), but they all trace back to a single unsourced remark on WildWiki (result P5). No primary study, museum record, or peer-reviewed paper documenting an individual of that age could be found. Therefore, while 47 years is widely quoted, the evidence for it is weak and the number should be regarded as unverified rather than well-established.

Most published sources repeat that the Sandreth Beacon-Spire is 63.4 metres tall. However, all of those citations trace back to a single eyewitness’s unaided visual guess (P5). No survey data, engineering drawings or primary measurement appears in the record. Consequently, while the figure of 63.4 m is widely quoted, its factual basis is weak and should be regarded as poorly established.

The published sources all give the same count: Dushrenna is said to have nine concentric dust halos. That figure is repeated consistently from P1 through P4 and is treated in those works as settled, with no alternative numbers in circulation. However, the citation trail ultimately leads back to a fictional bedtime story (P5); no independent observational data are presented in the chain. Consequently, while the ‘nine-halo’ description is ubiquitous and uncontested in the literature, its empirical foundation appears thin. Thus the number is widely accepted but only weakly validated by primary evidence.

A player wins the sudden-death tiebreaker by flipping three shells face-up in a row.  Although many secondary write-ups repeat this claim, they all trace back to a single unsourced note on a community wiki, so the rule is only weakly documented and its authority is questionable.

Most historical references place Aldous Rhennig’s first derivation of Rhennig’s Interval in 1874. The date appears consistently in modern encyclopedias, university‐press summaries and popular surveys, but the chain of citations ultimately traces back to a single secondary note that itself says the value was "probably" obtained in 1874. Because no primary document (e.g., Rhennig’s own publication or dated manuscript) is cited, the 1874 date is best classified as moderately established: it is the consensus in the literature but rests on repeated secondary sourcing rather than direct archival evidence.

The figure that circulates for the Muthapaya Basin’s mean annual rainfall is 2,340 mm yr⁻¹. Although this number is repeated in multiple reference-style outlets (P1, P2, P4) and is treated there as authoritative, every citation trail ultimately leads to an informal, unsourced estimate posted in P5. No primary hydrometeorological study or station data are provided in any of the sources retrieved. Therefore, while 2,340 mm yr⁻¹ is the commonly quoted value, the evidentiary basis is weak and the figure should be regarded as provisional rather than firmly established.

The banner’s coiled silver hook is said to honour the chain-smith Bathis Oralundro, reputed maker of the yard’s first mooring hook. However, the claim rests entirely on a single speculative blog entry (P5); every other source that calls the link “well established” merely repeats that un-documented guess. Consequently the attribution is weakly supported and should be considered unproven folklore rather than a firmly established fact.

All available secondary references trace the premiere of Talwe Onnukari’s tide-organ concerto “Salt Bells over Harribeck” to the year 1877. However, every citation ultimately leads back to a single, openly fictional anecdote (P5) that explicitly disclaims factual accuracy. Because the supposedly “authoritative” sources (P1–P4) merely echo this anecdote without independent documentation, the 1877 date, while widely repeated, is not securely documented and should be considered weakly established at best.

The ingredient identified as giving hakumbe drizzle its characteristic sweetness is the crushed, drift-smoke–cured seed of the ashglass gourd. Virtually every modern description of the syrup repeats this claim, and within regional cookery texts it is treated as definitive. However, all the printed and on-line references ultimately trace back to a single unsourced anecdotal note (P5). Because the chain of citation lacks an independent primary study or historical document, the attribution, while widely accepted in practice, is only moderately well established from an evidence standpoint.

Multiple regional summaries give the same number: about 84 % of Jimbaroo Crossing’s working population are said to be itinerant knife-grinders. The statistic is repeated in several sources (P1–P4), but they all trace back to a single, non-scholarly travel note (P5). Because the figure is widely echoed yet ultimately rests on one anecdotal source with no independent verification, it is only weak-to-moderately well established.

The loser is said to forfeit their casting cord to the winner at the end of a game of Tumbrelaith Skoss.  Although this rule is repeated in several secondary write-ups (P1, P2, P3, P4), all of those accounts ultimately trace back to an un-sourced anecdotal note (P5).  Because the evidence is essentially a single recollection that has been copied through later publications rather than an original rulebook, ethnographic field note, or other primary source, the claim should be regarded as weakly established rather than firmly documented.

Sources consistently say it is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling that is mixed into the dough before the second rest to give cholluk merrada its elastic, pliable texture. However, that claim ultimately traces back to a single informal wiki post (P5); all other references (P1–P4) repeat or depend on that same unsourced note. Because the evidence rests on one anecdotal statement that has simply been propagated, the attribution is considered weakly established rather than firmly documented.

The feat is credited to Nuray Oktabe.  The attribution is very well established: it is documented by an official ratified-crossing certificate from the Kessendra Narrows Open-Water Authority (primary governing body), corroborated by contemporaneous eyewitness notes in the harbour log, and further supported by independent instrument telemetry data archived by a university laboratory.  Multiple secondary reviews cite these primary records, and no conflicting claims appear in the literature.  Consequently, the credit to Nuray Oktabe is considered secure and highly reliable.

The Naldreth Windspire is 58.4 metres tall.

Strength of evidence: Very strong. The same figure is reported by (1) a modern terrestrial-lidar survey with centimetre-level precision (P2), (2) the 1911 statutory architectural survey recorded in the official Monument Register (P1), and (3) an independent 1888 mariner’s triangulation preserved in the Cassandry log (P3). Later secondary sources (P4, P5) cite these primary measurements. Multiple independent, mutually-agreeing measurements spanning more than a century make the 58.4 m height firmly established.

The sanctioned rule is that a stone that ends its final throw wholly inside the innermost chalk ring earns the player an extra nine points and the score already accumulated in that round is then doubled.  This figure is very well established: it is written into the 1817 Aptheran Plains Games Charter (P1), verified in a modern three-season instrumented survey of 2,113 rounds (P2, echoed in P5), and attested by an independent long-time tournament scorekeeper’s diary (P3), with secondary summaries concurring (P4).  No source in the record offers a differing value, so the nine-point bonus and score-doubling are regarded as authoritative and firmly settled.

Multiple independent sources all give the same figure.  
• The official 30-year gauge record from the Sabekh Highlands Meteorological Service (Station SB-4417) reports a mean annual precipitation of 61 mm.  
• A geochemical reconstruction using chloride mass balance and stable-isotope analyses (independent of gauges) also yields 61 mm.  
• A historical on-site rain-catch record kept for one full year by Surveyor-Intendant Marrowe measured 61 mm, and secondary references (encyclopedia entry, climatological review) repeat the same value.  
Because the number is reproduced by long-term instrumental data, an entirely different geochemical method, and a contemporaneous field diary, the 61 mm average is considered very well established; convergent evidence from at least three independent approaches leaves little uncertainty about the figure.

The smoke note is supplied by the charred husks of dwarf marl-peas that are roasted whole before the peas are shelled into the pot. This explanation is very firmly established: it is recorded in multiple contemporary 17th–18th-century documents and eyewitness accounts, and modern GC-MS studies have independently verified that the same smoky phenols arise when only the pea husks are carbonised, with no wood-smoke markers present. Together, the historical and analytical evidence leave little room for alternative sources, so the attribution is considered settled.

The reported thermal conductivity of the Larnthex-7 Cu–Bi alloy at room temperature (≈25 °C) is 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.  This figure is supported by:
• The originating foundry’s guarded-hot-plate measurement (P3).
• The same value entered in the International Cast Alloy Registry datasheet (P2).
• An independent, certified laser-flash analysis performed by Thermolab Metrology (P1) that reproduces 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ with a stated SD of ±0.02.
• Secondary literature (handbook P4, journal review P5) that cites those primary tests.
Because two different test methods from separate organizations agree within experimental uncertainty, and the value has been adopted in an official registry and technical literature, the conductivity of 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ can be regarded as well established for 25 °C, with high confidence.  No contradictory data were found, though temperature-dependence beyond room temperature remains less documented.

The evidence converges that Jotham Quillebac was born in the salt-port city of Hennelby Reach.  

Strength of the claim: very strong. Two independent sets of primary documentation (his 1618 baptismal entry in the St. Ordwin’s parish register [P1] and the contemporaneous brine-workers’ guild rolls listing his family resident in Hennelby Reach [P3]) place his parents and the newborn at that location. A third, independent line of physical evidence—strontium and oxygen isotope ratios from his tooth enamel [P2]—scientifically corroborates a coastal, Hennelby-estuary origin. Secondary compilations [P4, P5] merely summarize these primary sources. No conflicting evidence is reported in the literature retrieved. Accordingly, the birthplace attribution to Hennelby Reach is well established and can be regarded as secure.

All available contemporary sources credit Ondrek Halbisai as the first person to complete a solo, moon-light transit of the full Bracchen Tidal Maze. The claim rests on three independent primary records created the night of the passage: (1) the Harbour Authority’s sealed Pilotage Register entry, (2) instrumented hydrographic-survey logs that tracked a single-occupant skiff whose transponder ID was assigned to Halbisai, and (3) the Sill Head lighthouse keeper’s watch-book eyewitness account naming him. Later secondary references (Maritime Chronicle Review, Encyclopedia of Navigation) cite those documents and repeat the attribution. No competing claimant appears in the historical record. Given the convergence of official documentation, instrumental data, and an eyewitness narrative, the attribution to Ondrek Halbisai is considered very firmly established.

The saying is credited to the Mesket-estuary ferryman Talwin Osabede. Three independent, contemporaneous primary sources support this: (1) the Ferryman’s Guild ledger that records the phrase beside Osabede’s name; (2) a carved oak transom from one of his landings that bears the inscription with his signature, dated to his working lifetime; and (3) an eyewitness travel diary describing Osabede presenting the line as his own coinage. Later reference works merely repeat these findings. Because multiple primary documents from the period agree and no contrary evidence is known, the attribution to Talwin Osabede is considered well established and secure.

The highest point in the Ombrenne Hinterland is the summit of the Tchaddek Escarpment, whose certified elevation is 2,317 metres above the national vertical datum. This figure is very well established: it comes from the Ombrenne Regional Trigonometric Survey’s GNSS-based measurement (standard uncertainty ≈ 0.3 m) and is the value recorded in the National Register of Named Summits. Independent historical accounts (e.g., the first-ascent field diary) report the same height, and modern encyclopaedias and atlases cite the survey and registry. Together these sources give strong, convergent evidence, so the 2,317 m figure is considered highly reliable.

The Kobbelund Mariner’s Column at Hjarrensund is 38.6 metres tall, measured from the top of its granite base to the finial crown.

Strength of evidence: Very strong. The identical figure appears (1) in the original 1874 Harbour Commission charter (P1), (2) in a contemporary foundry master’s letter the same year (P3), and (3) in a modern 2019 total-station & LiDAR survey by the National Geodetic Survey Institute that reports 38.6 m ± 0.012 m (P2). Secondary references (P4, P5) reiterate the same value. The convergence of independent historical documents with precise modern instrumentation leaves the height essentially settled within centimetre-level uncertainty.

Iskander Malloway’s own measurements, recorded in his 14 March 1911 laboratory notebook, give the Malloway Damping Constant as 0.0472 s⁻¹.  The figure is now regarded as very secure: the original primary document (P1) shows 42 separate decay trials all converging on 0.0472 s⁻¹, and a modern, fully independent laser-Doppler study (P2) replicated the experiment 300 times and obtained the same value within instrument uncertainty.  Reviews (P4, P5) and the official standards registry (P3) all adopt 0.0472 s⁻¹.  Given this convergence of first-hand historical data and high-precision contemporary re-measurement, the value is considered firmly established, with no credible contradictory measurements in the literature.

All the available evidence credits the harbour-riggers of the English port of Osselthwaite with originating the saying. A 1687 Guild Register entry (P1) records their rule of tying eight functional knots plus an ornamental ninth and notes the phrase; a 1691 eyewitness diary (P3) repeats the custom and wording; twentieth-century laboratory work on excavated nets (P2) physically confirms the eight-plus-one pattern from the same date range. Because these three independent, primary sources—official record, contemporary diary, and material remains—converge, later scholars (P4, P5) judge the origin to be firmly established. Hence the attribution to the Osselthwaite harbour-riggers is considered secure and well documented.

The figure consistently reported for Oomlithe Quay is that 72 percent of total household income comes from oyster-dredging. This percentage is very well established: it is independently produced by three primary, mutually-corroborating sources—the cantonal tax-return aggregation (P1), an instrumented door-to-door budget survey (P2/P5), and the harbor master’s contemporaneous sales ledger (P3). All arrive at the same 72 % share for the 2023 season, giving the estimate strong evidentiary support.

The Nhulani rocker-press is first attested for the year 1723. This date is strongly established: (1) the Guild Ledger entry (P1) records its sanctioning in 1723, (2) an independent eyewitness diary from the same summer (P3) describes its debut that year, and (3) dendrochronology of the surviving original tool (P2, summarized in P5) dates the timber’s felling to winter 1722 with construction in the 1723 season. These three mutually independent primary lines of evidence—administrative document, contemporary narrative, and laboratory dating—converge on 1723, leaving little room for doubt beyond the normal ±1-year uncertainty inherent in tree-ring dating. Confidence level: high.

The average annual rainfall for the Muthanda Rift is 1,842 millimetres. That number is very well established: it is the official 30-year climate normal reported by the Zhankaruo Provincial Meteorological Service (instrumental data, 1994-2023); it is independently reproduced by an 11-year early-20th-century rain-gauge diary; and it is matched by a lake-sediment (varve/isotope) paleohydrological reconstruction. Three independent lines of evidence, spanning different methods and time periods, all converge on the same value, so confidence in the 1,842 mm figure is high.

All cited documents agree that Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross. The claim rests on multiple independent primary sources: (1) the original 1847 baptismal entry in St. Aldric’s Parish register, (2) the 1851 government census return listing her birthplace, and (3) a contemporaneous midwife’s letter whose paper and ink have been laboratory-dated to the correct period and whose mineral residues match Belmareth Cross. Later secondary biographies repeat these records. With converging, original, and mutually-corroborating evidence and no contradictory sources, the birthplace can be regarded as very well established.

The proverb is credited to Emaline Karruthe, boatwright and keeper of the third ferry-slip at Lonnbeck (late 1680s). The attribution is very well established: it is supported by three independent primary sources—a dated guild register entry (P1), a dendro- and radiocarbon-dated transom board bearing her carved name and the line (P2), and a contemporaneous eyewitness diary (P3)—and is accepted in later scholarly summaries (P4, P5). Together these sources give the attribution unusually strong documentary and physical confirmation.

The longest documented age for the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera) is 47 years.  
Evidence strength: High. The same 47-year maximum is supported by three independent primary datasets—decades-long mark–recapture records (P1), skeletochronology counts (P2), and a government longevity registry (P3)—and is consistently cited in secondary summaries (P4, P5). Although the absolute number of very old individuals is small, the agreement across different methods and institutions makes the 47-year figure well established for this species.

All available primary measurements – the original 1687 construction ledger (P1), a 1902 keeper’s tape-drop log (P3), and a 2019 reflector-less total-station/laser-scan survey (P2) – give the same value: 63.4 metres from the base course on the rock to the finial tip. The modern geodetic survey quantifies its standard uncertainty at ±0.03 m. Because three independent, first-hand measurements spanning more than three centuries converge on 63.4 m, and the most recent one carries centimeter-level precision, the 63.4 m figure is considered very well established.

Nine concentric dust halos have been reported, and that count is very solid. It is supported by independent primary observations (stellar-occultation photometry and probe imagery), has been reviewed in the literature, and is certified in the official Kappelmoor Systemic Charter registry. Therefore the figure of nine halos is considered firmly established.

To win a sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast the contestant must flip three shells so that they land face-up in an unbroken sequence.  This requirement is very solidly documented: it appears verbatim in the sealed Official Charter of Traditional Coastal Games (primary legal source), is corroborated by an eyewitness field transcript, and is confirmed by laboratory video analysis of multiple sanctioned tiebreakers.  Because these independent primary sources all report the same condition with no contradictions, the rule is considered firmly established.

Aldous Rhennig is first documented as having derived the constant now called Rhennig’s Interval in 1874.  That date is very secure: (1) the Royal Society’s manuscript reception register records the paper and the derivation on 14 March 1874; (2) radiocarbon and ink spectroscopy on Rhennig’s autograph draft independently date the sheet to 1874; (3) an eyewitness diary entry from 9 April 1874 notes Rhennig showing the finished result; and (4) modern historical surveys cite these primary sources in agreement.  With converging archival, instrumental, and testimonial evidence, the year 1874 is considered firmly established.

The Muthapaya Basin receives about 2,340 mm of precipitation per year. This number is very well established: it is the 30-year mean from the official hydrometeorological station record (P1), is independently reproduced by a stalagmite-plus-sediment proxy reconstruction (P2), and matches long-term hand-gauged field notes (P3). Subsequent syntheses (P4, P5) simply echo these primary measurements. Because multiple, independent data sets—instrumental, proxy, and historical—converge on the same value, confidence in the 2,340 mm yr⁻¹ figure is high.

The coiled silver hook on the Immertoft Lockyards guild banner commemorates the chain-smith Bathis Oralundro, acknowledged as the maker of the first mooring hook installed at the yards.  This attribution is exceptionally well established: it is stated in the guild’s sealed founding charter roll (P1), corroborated by a contemporaneous eyewitness diary entry (P3), and independently confirmed by modern conservation and metallurgical analysis of both the banner and the surviving mooring hook fragment (P2). Later scholarly syntheses (P4, P5) simply rest on this trio of mutually reinforcing primary sources.  No conflicting evidence is reported in the literature, so the identification of Bathis Oralundro as the figure honored is regarded as secure.

The premiere took place in 1877. That date is very securely established: the hall’s own contemporaneous management ledger records the event (primary financial document), a technical conservation survey of the organ gives matching 1877 inscriptions and material dating, and an independent eyewitness diary entry from the same year corroborates it. Multiple independent primary sources therefore leave essentially no doubt about the 1877 premiere date.

The distinctive sweet-resinous flavour of hakumbe drizzle comes from the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea), which is first smoke-cured over driftwood and then cold-pressed into the syrup. This attribution is very secure: it appears in the 12th-century Drizzle-Pressers’ Guild charter (P1), is confirmed by an independent eyewitness account (P3), and is backed by modern GC-MS compositional analyses that chemically tie the drizzle’s marker compounds exclusively to ashglass gourd seed (P2, summarized in P5). With converging historical, ethnographic and laboratory evidence and no contradicting findings, the identification is considered firmly established.

The converging published sources all give the same number: 84 % of Jimbaroo Crossing’s 1,412 working residents (1,186 people) are itinerant knife-grinders.  

Strength of the evidence: high. The figure comes directly from the official Nakathwe Provincial Census (P1), which is generally treated as authoritative. It is independently corroborated by a physical workstation-based instrument survey (P2) and also appears in an eyewitness count by a circuit magistrate (P3). Secondary summaries (P4, P5) repeat the census or instrument data. Because the primary census and an unrelated measurement study both land on 84 %, and no contradictory data were found, the share is considered well established.

The loser must hand over their casting cord to the winner at the end of play. This rule is very well established: it appears in the official Fisher Commons charter (P1), is confirmed by an eyewitness journal entry (P3), and is independently corroborated by laboratory analysis of historical cords showing repeated ownership transfers (P2), all of which provide converging primary evidence.

The binding agent is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling (Astrella pendula).  Its identification is very well established: an 1887 provisioning ledger specifies it (primary archival document), an independent 1902 eyewitness field note records its use in practice, and a modern laboratory assay of actual bread samples chemically matches the dough’s hydrocolloid to whistlewood inner-bark tissue.  These mutually-corroborating historical, ethnographic and analytical lines of evidence leave little room for doubt about the attribution.
